title: Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy
excerpt: On November 24, 2026, the non-profit DNS resolver Quad9 stops serving users in France rather than obey a beIN Sports blocking order. Here's what Quad9 is, how the French law got here, and why forcing public resolvers to block domains breaks more than it fixes.
content_html:
On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.

Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.

What Quad9 is, and why it matters​

A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.

Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:

  • It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House, and moved its legal seat to Zürich in 2021, hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises."
  • Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries.
  • It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point.

Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working."

How France got here​

The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport​

The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).

That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026, Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous."

The cases: from ISPs to everyone​

The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened:

DateWhat happened
Dec 2023Canal+ sues Cloudflare, Google and Cisco under L.333-10 to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites.
May–Jun 2024The Paris court orders the three resolvers to block ~117 domains. Google complies. Cisco pulls OpenDNS out of France on June 28, 2024, citing a court order "issued under Article L.333-10 of the French Sport code" (archived notice).
Sep–Oct 2024New orders expand blocking by Google and Cloudflare.
Dec 2024Canal+ wins three orders against Quad9 and Vercara (Premier League, Champions League, Top 14 rugby). Because it can't geolocate users, Quad9 blocks the domains for the whole world: "we have to block these sites for all users, in all areas."
May 2025A beIN request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 is rejected for lack of evidence. Quad9 didn't defend that case at all, citing lack of resources.
Mar 2026The Paris Court of Appeal rejects five appeals by Google, Cloudflare and Cisco (RG 24/09372), the first appellate approval of DNS blocking under L.333-10: "Any filtering measure can be circumvented, and this possibility does not render the measures in question ineffective." The same month, the court issues simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers.
Apr 2026Canal+ obtains orders against Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver, which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers."
May 13, 2026beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the WTA women's tennis tour until the season ends on November 14. It starts with 6 domains and grows to 58 via Arcom notifications.
Jul 202614 new Canal+ orders for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing.
Oct 7, 2026The court refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare kept 1.1.1.1 out of it by acting through its CDN instead.
Oct 21, 2026The court imposes a €1,000/day penalty on Quad9 (RG 26/11882).
Oct 22, 2026Quad9 announces it will leave France on November 24.

The ruling itself​

The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter:

  • The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for €10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14.
  • The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France.
  • Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty."

€1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases."

Why Quad9 can't just comply​

Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.

1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.

2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.

3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat."

That leaves leaving.

Why DNS blocking doesn't work​

The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.

It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing.

It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert."

It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)

It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.

Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.

Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events."

What France loses​

Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.

  • French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web."
  • Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix.
  • The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver.
  • France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain.

How other countries block, and what is different about France​

Governments have used DNS to block websites for years. What is new about the French sports cases is not the technique but who is ordered to carry it out, and how far the block reaches.

Turkey: block at home, intercept the rest​

In April 2017, Turkey's telecoms regulator BTK blocked all of Wikipedia under Article 8/A of Law 5651, approved the same day by an Ankara criminal judgeship of peace. Turkish ISPs implemented it with DNS spoofing plus connection filtering. The regulator said blocking only the offending pages was "technically impossible", so it blocked the whole site. The Constitutional Court ruled 10–6 in December 2019 that the block violated freedom of expression, and access returned in January 2020.

The more relevant precedent is Turkey's 2014 Twitter ban. It started as a DNS block on Turkish ISPs' resolvers, and people responded by spray-painting Google's DNS addresses on walls. Turkey did not ask Google to block anything. Instead, Google reported that "Google's Public DNS service has been intercepted by most Turkish ISPs", which had "set up servers that masquerade as Google's DNS service." When Cloudflare launched 1.1.1.1 in 2018, Turkish networks silently dropped its Wikipedia lookups the same way they did for Google and Quad9.

Turkey's approach is heavy-handed, but it is domestic. The state makes its own ISPs tamper with traffic inside Turkey. France instead orders a foreign resolver to change the answers it gives, and because the resolver can't reliably tell who is French, the block either goes global or the resolver leaves.

United States: take the domain away for everyone​

The US does not block sites through ISPs or resolvers. It seizes the domain. A federal judge issues a forfeiture warrant (the banner above cites 18 U.S.C. § 981(b)), and the registry, such as Verisign for .com in Virginia, points the domain at government name servers. Z-Library's domains went this way in November 2022. Operation In Our Sites seized 2,713 domains between 2010 and early 2014, and in July 2026 the Justice Department seized more than 1,000 World Cup streaming sites.

A seizure is more drastic than anything France does: the domain stops working worldwide, for every resolver. But it acts on the alleged wrongdoer's own property, through the registry that holds the record, and it says so. Anyone who visits sees a banner naming the court, the agency and the statute. Nobody unconnected to the site is fined.

The US has never had a court site-blocking regime. SOPA and PIPA were shelved in January 2012 after mass protests. In September 2026, two newer bills were merged into the DEFEND IP Act, which would cover ISPs and public DNS resolvers with more than $100 million in annual revenue. That threshold would leave a small non-profit like Quad9 out of scope. The bill has not had a committee vote and the EFF opposes it.

United Kingdom: ISPs, and only ISPs​

UK copyright blocking began with Newzbin2 in 2011, when the High Court ordered BT to block the site using its Cleanfeed system, which the court described as "IP address re-routing and DPI-based URL blocking". In 2017 the Premier League won the first live blocking order against the six main ISPs. It blocks streaming servers only while matches are on, with the server list "re-set" each week. That is the same dynamic, match-day model France uses, but aimed only at the companies that connect UK customers.

The UK's approach to pornography is different again. A plan to require age checks under the Digital Economy Act 2017 was dropped in 2019. The Online Safety Act's age checks took effect on July 25, 2025, and Proton VPN saw UK sign-ups jump more than 1,400%. Ofcom enforces the rules against the sites themselves, with fines such as £1 million against AVS Group, and it fined one site that had geoblocked the UK. The Act lets Ofcom ask a court for an access restriction order binding ISPs, but as of November 2026 it has not sought one.

Before either of those, ISPs switched on default "family filters" in 2013 and block the Internet Watch Foundation's child abuse list, with the IWF leaving each ISP to choose the method and recommending a splash page that tells users why.

We found no UK order against a public DNS resolver. When Cloudflare started blocking pirate sites for UK users in 2025, it did so through its CDN with an HTTP 451 page, not through 1.1.1.1.

France's other blocking regimes​

France itself blocked through ISPs for a decade before the sports cases.

  • Terrorism and child abuse. Since a 2015 decree, police keep a list of sites that ISPs must block within 24 hours, redirecting users to an Interior Ministry warning page. No judge is involved. In October 2016, a "human error" at Orange sent users of Google.fr and Wikipedia to that terrorism page.
  • Copyright. Courts ordered six French ISPs to block the Allostreaming sites in 2013, and four ISPs to block 57 Sci-Hub and LibGen domains in 2019. OONI counts Arcom's mirror-site procedure "used 88 times in 2023 to block 549 domains", all through ISPs.
  • TikTok in New Caledonia. In May 2024 the government had the territory's single ISP block TikTok during riots. The Conseil d'État later ruled that the open-ended block was a disproportionate interference.
  • Pornography. Under the 2024 SREN law, Arcom can order blocking of porn sites without age checks, and the law names "fournisseurs de systèmes de résolution de noms de domaine" (DNS resolver providers) alongside ISPs. In March 2025, Arcom ordered Cloudflare to block camschat.net through its resolver within 48 hours. This was an administrative order with no judge, and the Paris administrative court rejected Cloudflare's challenge. Aylo pulled Pornhub out of France in June 2025 rather than comply.

The porn case shows that resolvers are no longer a sports-only target in France. The resolver obligation is now written into a general law.

Side by side​

CaseWho does the blockingWhere it appliesWhat the user seesWho decides
Turkey, Wikipedia (2017)Turkish ISPs, intercepting foreign resolversTurkeyErrorsRegulator, approved by a judge
US domain seizuresThe domain registryWorldwideSeizure banner naming the courtFederal judge (warrant)
UK copyrightUK ISPsUKVaries by ISPHigh Court
UK Online Safety ActThe site itself (fines)UKThe site's own pageOfcom
France, terrorismFrench ISPsFranceInterior Ministry pagePolice, no judge
France, porn (SREN)ISPs and DNS resolversFranceArcom pageArcom, no judge
France, sports (Quad9)Any resolver, foreign or notWorldwide, unless the resolver can geolocateNothing; the site just failsJudge, plus Arcom adding domains

What's the same, and what isn't​

The similarities are real. Every one of these regimes uses lists that grow over time, every one hits legitimate content when it blocks a whole domain (Wikipedia in Turkey, Google.fr at Orange), and every DNS-based one is defeated by switching resolver or encrypting DNS.

The differences explain why Quad9 is leaving:

  1. The target is a bystander. Turkey, the UK and earlier France order the user's own ISP. The US acts on the domain itself. The French sports orders go after a third party that neither connects the user nor hosts the site.
  2. The target is foreign and has no local network. An ISP knows its customers are in its country. A global resolver doesn't, so a national order turns into a global one by default. That gives a French judge something close to the worldwide reach of a US seizure, without the seizure's basis in the site's own wrongdoing.
  3. The user isn't told. The US shows a banner, French terrorism blocks show a ministry page, and Arcom's porn orders redirect to an Arcom page. The sports orders require none of this.
  4. The penalty falls on the intermediary. UK porn enforcement fines the site. The French sports regime fines the resolver, daily, for refusing to change answers about sites it has nothing to do with.

Even Turkey, whose blocking record France would not want to be compared with, kept its blocking inside its own networks.

It's not just France​

Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe.

  • Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order, with fines of €100,000 per match day capped at €20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline.
  • Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare €14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."
  • Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses.
  • Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare.
  • The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region."

That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.

The counter-arguments​

The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.

"Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.

"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.

"Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie.

"The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.

What you can do​

If you use Quad9 in France, check whether you do at on.quad9.net, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first.

If you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage."

If you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.

If you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.

The canary​

Quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.

The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.

The same month, the court issues simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers.Apr 2026Canal+ obtains orders against Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver, which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers."May 13, 2026beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the WTA women's tennis tour until the season ends on November 14. It starts with 6 domains and grows to 58 via Arcom notifications.Jul 202614 new Canal+ orders for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing.Oct 7, 2026The court refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare kept 1.1.1.1 out of it by acting through its CDN instead.Oct 21, 2026The court imposes a €1,000/day penalty on Quad9 (RG 26/11882).Oct 22, 2026Quad9 announces it will leave France on November 24. The ruling itself​ The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter: The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for €10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14. The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France. Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty." €1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases." Why Quad9 can't just comply​ Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work. 1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver. 2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia. 3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat." That leaves leaving. Why DNS blocking doesn't work​ The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want. It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing. It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert." It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.) It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it. Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider. Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events." What France loses​ Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security. French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web." Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix. The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver. France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain. How other countries block, and what is different about France​ Governments have used DNS to block websites for years. What is new about the French sports cases is not the technique but who is ordered to carry it out, and how far the block reaches. Turkey: block at home, intercept the rest​ In April 2017, Turkey's telecoms regulator BTK blocked all of Wikipedia under Article 8/A of Law 5651, approved the same day by an Ankara criminal judgeship of peace. Turkish ISPs implemented it with DNS spoofing plus connection filtering. The regulator said blocking only the offending pages was "technically impossible", so it blocked the whole site. The Constitutional Court ruled 10–6 in December 2019 that the block violated freedom of expression, and access returned in January 2020. The more relevant precedent is Turkey's 2014 Twitter ban. It started as a DNS block on Turkish ISPs' resolvers, and people responded by spray-painting Google's DNS addresses on walls. Turkey did not ask Google to block anything. Instead, Google reported that "Google's Public DNS service has been intercepted by most Turkish ISPs", which had "set up servers that masquerade as Google's DNS service." When Cloudflare launched 1.1.1.1 in 2018, Turkish networks silently dropped its Wikipedia lookups the same way they did for Google and Quad9. Turkey's approach is heavy-handed, but it is domestic. The state makes its own ISPs tamper with traffic inside Turkey. France instead orders a foreign resolver to change the answers it gives, and because the resolver can't reliably tell who is French, the block either goes global or the resolver leaves. United States: take the domain away for everyone​ The US does not block sites through ISPs or resolvers. It seizes the domain. A federal judge issues a forfeiture warrant (the banner above cites 18 U.S.C. § 981(b)), and the registry, such as Verisign for .com in Virginia, points the domain at government name servers. Z-Library's domains went this way in November 2022. Operation In Our Sites seized 2,713 domains between 2010 and early 2014, and in July 2026 the Justice Department seized more than 1,000 World Cup streaming sites. A seizure is more drastic than anything France does: the domain stops working worldwide, for every resolver. But it acts on the alleged wrongdoer's own property, through the registry that holds the record, and it says so. Anyone who visits sees a banner naming the court, the agency and the statute. Nobody unconnected to the site is fined. The US has never had a court site-blocking regime. SOPA and PIPA were shelved in January 2012 after mass protests. In September 2026, two newer bills were merged into the DEFEND IP Act, which would cover ISPs and public DNS resolvers with more than $100 million in annual revenue. That threshold would leave a small non-profit like Quad9 out of scope. The bill has not had a committee vote and the EFF opposes it. United Kingdom: ISPs, and only ISPs​ UK copyright blocking began with Newzbin2 in 2011, when the High Court ordered BT to block the site using its Cleanfeed system, which the court described as "IP address re-routing and DPI-based URL blocking". In 2017 the Premier League won the first live blocking order against the six main ISPs. It blocks streaming servers only while matches are on, with the server list "re-set" each week. That is the same dynamic, match-day model France uses, but aimed only at the companies that connect UK customers. The UK's approach to pornography is different again. A plan to require age checks under the Digital Economy Act 2017 was dropped in 2019. The Online Safety Act's age checks took effect on July 25, 2025, and Proton VPN saw UK sign-ups jump more than 1,400%. Ofcom enforces the rules against the sites themselves, with fines such as £1 million against AVS Group, and it fined one site that had geoblocked the UK. The Act lets Ofcom ask a court for an access restriction order binding ISPs, but as of November 2026 it has not sought one. Before either of those, ISPs switched on default "family filters" in 2013 and block the Internet Watch Foundation's child abuse list, with the IWF leaving each ISP to choose the method and recommending a splash page that tells users why. We found no UK order against a public DNS resolver. When Cloudflare started blocking pirate sites for UK users in 2025, it did so through its CDN with an HTTP 451 page, not through 1.1.1.1. France's other blocking regimes​ France itself blocked through ISPs for a decade before the sports cases. Terrorism and child abuse. Since a 2015 decree, police keep a list of sites that ISPs must block within 24 hours, redirecting users to an Interior Ministry warning page. No judge is involved. In October 2016, a "human error" at Orange sent users of Google.fr and Wikipedia to that terrorism page. Copyright. Courts ordered six French ISPs to block the Allostreaming sites in 2013, and four ISPs to block 57 Sci-Hub and LibGen domains in 2019. OONI counts Arcom's mirror-site procedure "used 88 times in 2023 to block 549 domains", all through ISPs. TikTok in New Caledonia. In May 2024 the government had the territory's single ISP block TikTok during riots. The Conseil d'État later ruled that the open-ended block was a disproportionate interference. Pornography. Under the 2024 SREN law, Arcom can order blocking of porn sites without age checks, and the law names "fournisseurs de systèmes de résolution de noms de domaine" (DNS resolver providers) alongside ISPs. In March 2025, Arcom ordered Cloudflare to block camschat.net through its resolver within 48 hours. This was an administrative order with no judge, and the Paris administrative court rejected Cloudflare's challenge. Aylo pulled Pornhub out of France in June 2025 rather than comply. The porn case shows that resolvers are no longer a sports-only target in France. The resolver obligation is now written into a general law. Side by side​ CaseWho does the blockingWhere it appliesWhat the user seesWho decidesTurkey, Wikipedia (2017)Turkish ISPs, intercepting foreign resolversTurkeyErrorsRegulator, approved by a judgeUS domain seizuresThe domain registryWorldwideSeizure banner naming the courtFederal judge (warrant)UK copyrightUK ISPsUKVaries by ISPHigh CourtUK Online Safety ActThe site itself (fines)UKThe site's own pageOfcomFrance, terrorismFrench ISPsFranceInterior Ministry pagePolice, no judgeFrance, porn (SREN)ISPs and DNS resolversFranceArcom pageArcom, no judgeFrance, sports (Quad9)Any resolver, foreign or notWorldwide, unless the resolver can geolocateNothing; the site just failsJudge, plus Arcom adding domains What's the same, and what isn't​ The similarities are real. Every one of these regimes uses lists that grow over time, every one hits legitimate content when it blocks a whole domain (Wikipedia in Turkey, Google.fr at Orange), and every DNS-based one is defeated by switching resolver or encrypting DNS. The differences explain why Quad9 is leaving: The target is a bystander. Turkey, the UK and earlier France order the user's own ISP. The US acts on the domain itself. The French sports orders go after a third party that neither connects the user nor hosts the site. The target is foreign and has no local network. An ISP knows its customers are in its country. A global resolver doesn't, so a national order turns into a global one by default. That gives a French judge something close to the worldwide reach of a US seizure, without the seizure's basis in the site's own wrongdoing. The user isn't told. The US shows a banner, French terrorism blocks show a ministry page, and Arcom's porn orders redirect to an Arcom page. The sports orders require none of this. The penalty falls on the intermediary. UK porn enforcement fines the site. The French sports regime fines the resolver, daily, for refusing to change answers about sites it has nothing to do with. Even Turkey, whose blocking record France would not want to be compared with, kept its blocking inside its own networks. It's not just France​ Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe. Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order, with fines of €100,000 per match day capped at €20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline. Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare €14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes." Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses. Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare. The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region." That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave. The counter-arguments​ The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers. "Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement. "Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy. "Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie. "The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator. What you can do​ If you use Quad9 in France, check whether you do at on.quad9.net, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first. If you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage." If you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network. If you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal. The canary​ Quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues. The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.

blocks.html_en: On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.

blocks.html_en: The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).

blocks.html_en: Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.

blocks.html_en: 1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.

blocks.html_en: Why DNS blocking doesn't work​

sentences.en: Why DNS blocking doesn't work​

blocks.html_en: The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.

blocks.html_en: It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing.

Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. blocks.html_en: It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)

blocks.html_en: Turkey: block at home, intercept the rest​

blocks.html_en: In April 2017, Turkey's telecoms regulator BTK blocked all of Wikipedia under Article 8/A of Law 5651, approved the same day by an Ankara criminal judgeship of peace. Turkish ISPs implemented it with DNS spoofing plus connection filtering. The regulator said blocking only the offending pages was "technically impossible", so it blocked the whole site. The Constitutional Court ruled 10–6 in December 2019 that the block violated freedom of expression, and access returned in January 2020.

content_html_zh:
On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.

Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.

What Quad9 is, and why it matters​

A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.

Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:

  • It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House, and moved its legal seat to Zürich in 2021, hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises."
  • Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries.
  • It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point.

Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working."

How France got here​

The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport​

The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).

That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026, Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous."

The cases: from ISPs to everyone​

The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened:

Dec 2023Canal+ sues Cloudflare, Google and Cisco under L.333-10 to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites.
May–Jun 2024The Paris court orders the three resolvers to block ~117 domains. Google complies. Cisco pulls OpenDNS out of France on June 28, 2024, citing a court order "issued under Article L.333-10 of the French Sport code" (archived notice).
Sep–Oct 2024New orders expand blocking by Google and Cloudflare.
Dec 2024Canal+ wins three orders against Quad9 and Vercara (Premier League, Champions League, Top 14 rugby). Because it can't geolocate users, Quad9 blocks the domains for the whole world: "we have to block these sites for all users, in all areas."
May 2025A beIN request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 is rejected for lack of evidence. Quad9 didn't defend that case at all, citing lack of resources.
Mar 2026The Paris Court of Appeal rejects five appeals by Google, Cloudflare and Cisco (RG 24/09372), the first appellate approval of DNS blocking under L.333-10: "Any filtering measure can be circumvented, and this possibility does not render the measures in question ineffective." The same month, the court issues simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers.
Apr 2026Canal+ obtains orders against Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver, which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers."
May 13, 2026beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the WTA women's tennis tour until the season ends on November 14. It starts with 6 domains and grows to 58 via Arcom notifications.
Jul 202614 new Canal+ orders for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing.
Oct 7, 2026The court refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare kept 1.1.1.1 out of it by acting through its CDN instead.
Oct 21, 2026The court imposes a €1,000/day penalty on Quad9 (RG 26/11882).
Oct 22, 2026Quad9 announces it will leave France on November 24.

The ruling itself​

The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter:

  • The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for €10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14.
  • The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France.
  • Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty."

€1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases."

Why Quad9 can't just comply​

Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.

1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.

2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.

3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat."

That leaves leaving.

Why DNS blocking doesn't work​

The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.

It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing.

It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert."

It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)

It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.

Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.

Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events."

What France loses​

Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.

  • French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web."
  • Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix.
  • The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver.
  • France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain.

How other countries block, and what is different about France​

Governments have used DNS to block websites for years. What is new about the French sports cases is not the technique but who is ordered to carry it out, and how far the block reaches.

Turkey: block at home, intercept the rest​

In April 2017, Turkey's telecoms regulator BTK blocked all of Wikipedia under Article 8/A of Law 5651, approved the same day by an Ankara criminal judgeship of peace. Turkish ISPs implemented it with DNS spoofing plus connection filtering. The regulator said blocking only the offending pages was "technically impossible", so it blocked the whole site. The Constitutional Court ruled 10–6 in December 2019 that the block violated freedom of expression, and access returned in January 2020.

The more relevant precedent is Turkey's 2014 Twitter ban. It started as a DNS block on Turkish ISPs' resolvers, and people responded by spray-painting Google's DNS addresses on walls. Turkey did not ask Google to block anything. Instead, Google reported that "Google's Public DNS service has been intercepted by most Turkish ISPs", which had "set up servers that masquerade as Google's DNS service." When Cloudflare launched 1.1.1.1 in 2018, Turkish networks silently dropped its Wikipedia lookups the same way they did for Google and Quad9.

Turkey's approach is heavy-handed, but it is domestic. The state makes its own ISPs tamper with traffic inside Turkey. France instead orders a foreign resolver to change the answers it gives, and because the resolver can't reliably tell who is French, the block either goes global or the resolver leaves.

United States: take the domain away for everyone​

The US does not block sites through ISPs or resolvers. It seizes the domain. A federal judge issues a forfeiture warrant (the banner above cites 18 U.S.C. § 981(b)), and the registry, such as Verisign for .com in Virginia, points the domain at government name servers. Z-Library's domains went this way in November 2022. Operation In Our Sites seized 2,713 domains between 2010 and early 2014, and in July 2026 the Justice Department seized more than 1,000 World Cup streaming sites.

A seizure is more drastic than anything France does: the domain stops working worldwide, for every resolver. But it acts on the alleged wrongdoer's own property, through the registry that holds the record, and it says so. Anyone who visits sees a banner naming the court, the agency and the statute. Nobody unconnected to the site is fined.

The US has never had a court site-blocking regime. SOPA and PIPA were shelved in January 2012 after mass protests. In September 2026, two newer bills were merged into the DEFEND IP Act, which would cover ISPs and public DNS resolvers with more than $100 million in annual revenue. That threshold would leave a small non-profit like Quad9 out of scope. The bill has not had a committee vote and the EFF opposes it.

United Kingdom: ISPs, and only ISPs​

UK copyright blocking began with Newzbin2 in 2011, when the High Court ordered BT to block the site using its Cleanfeed system, which the court described as "IP address re-routing and DPI-based URL blocking". In 2017 the Premier League won the first live blocking order against the six main ISPs. It blocks streaming servers only while matches are on, with the server list "re-set" each week. That is the same dynamic, match-day model France uses, but aimed only at the companies that connect UK customers.

The UK's approach to pornography is different again. A plan to require age checks under the Digital Economy Act 2017 was dropped in 2019. The Online Safety Act's age checks took effect on July 25, 2025, and Proton VPN saw UK sign-ups jump more than 1,400%. Ofcom enforces the rules against the sites themselves, with fines such as £1 million against AVS Group, and it fined one site that had geoblocked the UK. The Act lets Ofcom ask a court for an access restriction order binding ISPs, but as of November 2026 it has not sought one.

Before either of those, ISPs switched on default "family filters" in 2013 and block the Internet Watch Foundation's child abuse list, with the IWF leaving each ISP to choose the method and recommending a splash page that tells users why.

We found no UK order against a public DNS resolver. When Cloudflare started blocking pirate sites for UK users in 2025, it did so through its CDN with an HTTP 451 page, not through 1.1.1.1.

France's other blocking regimes​

France itself blocked through ISPs for a decade before the sports cases.

  • Terrorism and child abuse. Since a 2015 decree, police keep a list of sites that ISPs must block within 24 hours, redirecting users to an Interior Ministry warning page. No judge is involved. In October 2016, a "human error" at Orange sent users of Google.fr and Wikipedia to that terrorism page.
  • Copyright. Courts ordered six French ISPs to block the Allostreaming sites in 2013, and four ISPs to block 57 Sci-Hub and LibGen domains in 2019. OONI counts Arcom's mirror-site procedure "used 88 times in 2023 to block 549 domains", all through ISPs.
  • TikTok in New Caledonia. In May 2024 the government had the territory's single ISP block TikTok during riots. The Conseil d'État later ruled that the open-ended block was a disproportionate interference.
  • Pornography. Under the 2024 SREN law, Arcom can order blocking of porn sites without age checks, and the law names "fournisseurs de systèmes de résolution de noms de domaine" (DNS resolver providers) alongside ISPs. In March 2025, Arcom ordered Cloudflare to block camschat.net through its resolver within 48 hours. This was an administrative order with no judge, and the Paris administrative court rejected Cloudflare's challenge. Aylo pulled Pornhub out of France in June 2025 rather than comply.

The porn case shows that resolvers are no longer a sports-only target in France. The resolver obligation is now written into a general law.
